nameStory: Sixweeks grass earned its name from cattle ranchers who noticed it provides about six weeks of decent forage after a good rain. This little annual grass grows fast, feeds livestock briefly, then disappears - making it a reliable but short-lived resource on rangeland. The name captures this plant's quick life cycle perfectly.
description: Sixweeks grass is a small annual grass that grows in delicate, wispy tufts usually 4-12 inches tall. It has very fine, thread-like leaves and produces tiny, inconspicuous flowers arranged in narrow clusters. This grass completes its entire life cycle quickly, often germinating, growing, flowering, and setting seed all within six weeks when conditions are right. It's easily overlooked unless you're specifically looking for small grasses.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms small, delicate tufts that feel wispy and fragile to the touch, often growing in scattered patches rather than dense mats

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Extremely narrow, thread-like leaves that roll inward and feel almost bristle-like when rubbed between your fingers

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny flowers arranged in narrow, spike-like clusters that are greenish or purplish and barely noticeable unless examined closely

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Small, light seeds that easily blow away or pull out of the seed head - hence another common name 'pullout grass'

idTips.label: Texture
idTips.description: Overall plant feels delicate and breakable, with a dry, almost papery texture even when alive

habitat: Look for sixweeks grass in disturbed, dry soils like roadsides, abandoned fields, sandy areas, and waste places throughout New England. It thrives in poor, well-drained soils where other plants struggle to establish. This grass is particularly common in areas with sandy or gravelly soil that heats up quickly in spring.

seasonality.spring: Seeds germinate early when soil warms, and young plants begin their rapid growth phase. Fresh green tufts appear in disturbed areas.
seasonality.summer: Plants flower, set seed, and often die back by midsummer, leaving dry, straw-colored remnants that persist.
seasonality.fall: Only dried seed heads and stems remain visible, easily breaking apart when touched.
seasonality.winter: Little to no visible remains above ground, as the plant completes its annual cycle and seeds wait for spring germination.

funFact: This grass can complete its entire life cycle - from seed to flowering to new seeds - in just six weeks, making it one of nature's ultimate sprint specialists that can take advantage of brief favorable conditions.
confusionNotes: Often confused with other small fescues, but sixweeks grass is much more delicate and breaks apart easily when handled, unlike the tougher perennial fescues. Remember: if it feels fragile and papery, it's likely sixweeks grass.
contextualKnowledge: This species is sometimes listed under the scientific name Vulpia octoflora in older field guides, which can cause confusion. Both names refer to the same plant - botanists have debated whether it belongs in the Festuca or Vulpia genus.
compareHints: Unlike its perennial fescue relatives like red fescue or sheep's fescue, sixweeks grass is much smaller, more delicate, and dies completely each year. While other fescues form persistent clumps that last for years, sixweeks grass creates temporary, wispy patches that appear and disappear seasonally. Its thread-like leaves are finer than most other fescues in the region.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among the fescues, rattail sixweeks grass is unique for its drooping seed heads - all other New England fescues like sheep's fescue and red fescue have upright or spreading flower clusters.
Among the fescues, sheep's fescue has the finest, most thread-like leaves - even thinner than hard fescue and much finer than red fescue.
Among the New England fescues, fine-leaved sheep's-fescue stands out for having the thinnest, most hair-like leaves - much finer than regular sheep's fescue or hard fescue.
Among the fescues in New England, red fescue is distinguished by its spreading growth habit via rhizomes, unlike the bunch-forming sheep's fescue or hard fescue.
Unlike its more common relatives like red fescue or sheep's fescue that prefer sunny, open areas, nodding fescue is the shade-lover of the family.
Among New England fescues, hard fescue stands out for its particularly coarse, rough leaf texture and tight clumping habit.
